source_text:
καὶ ἀλλαχοῦ· »ὁ ὑμᾶς δεχόμενος ἐμὲ δέχεται, ὁ ὑμᾶς μὴ δεχόμενος ἐμὲ ἀθετεῖ.«
Τούτους καὶ τέκνα καὶ παιδία καὶ νήπια καὶ φίλους ὀνομάζει καὶ μικροὺς ἐνθάδε ὡς πρὸς τὸ μέλλον ἄνω μέγεθος αὐτῶν. »μὴ καταφρονήσητε« λέγων »ἑνὸς τῶν μικρῶν τούτων· τούτων γὰρ οἱ ἄγγελοι διὰ παντὸς βλέπουσι τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ πατρός μου τοῦ ἐν οὐρανοῖς.« καὶ ἑτέρωθι· »μὴ φοβεῖσθε. τὸ μικρὸν ποίμνιον· ὑμῖν γὰρ εὐδόκησεν ὁ πατὴρ παραδοῦναι τὴν βασιλείαν« τῶν οὐρανῶν. κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ τοῦ μεγίστου ἐν γεννητοῖς γυναικῶν Ἰωάννου τὸν ἐλάχιστον ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν, τουτέστι τὸν ἑαυτοῦ μαθητήν, εἶναι μείζω λέγει. καὶ πάλιν· »ὁ δεχόμενος δίκαιον ἢ προφήτην εἰς ὄνομα δικαίου ἢ προφήτου τὸν ἐκείνων μισθὸν λήψεται. ὁ δὲ μαθητὴν ποτίσας εἰς ὄνομα μαθητοῦ ποτήριον ψυχροῦ ὕδατος τὸν μισθὸν οὐκ ἀπολέσει.« οὐκοῦν οὗτος μόνος ὁ μισθὸς οὐκ ἀπολλύμενός ἐστι. καὶ αὖθις· »ποιήσατε ἑαυτοῖς φίλους ἐκ τοῦ μαμωνᾶ τῆς ἀδικίας. ἵνα ὅταν ἐκλίπῃ, δέξωνται ὑμᾶς εἰς τὰς αἰωνίους σκηνάς.« φύσει μὲν ἅπασαν κτῆσιν, ἣν αὐτός τις ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ κέκτηται ὡς ἰδίαν οὖσαν καὶ οὐκ εἰς κοινὸν τοῖς δεομένοις κατατίθησιν, ἄδικον οὖσαν ἀποφαίνων, ἐκ δὲ ταύτης τῆς ἀδικίας ἐνὸν καὶ πρᾶγμα δίκαιον ἐργάσασθαι καὶ σωτήριον, ἀναπαῦσαί τινα τῶν ἐχόντων αἰώνιον σκηνὴν παρὰ τῷ πατρί.
Ὅρα πρῶτον μὲν ὡς οὐκ ἀπαιτεῖσθαί σε κεκέλευκεν οὐδὲ ἐνοχλεῖσθαι περιμένειν, ἀλλὰ αὐτὸν ζητεῖν τοὺς εὖ πεισομένους ἀξίους τε ὄντας τοῦ σωτῆρος μαθητάς, καλὸς μὲν οὖν καὶ ὁ τοῦ ἀποστόλου λόγος· »ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός«, χαίροντα τῷ διδόναι καὶ μὴ φειδομένως σπείροντα, ἵνα μὴ οὕτως καὶ θερίσῃ. δίχα γογγυσμῶν καὶ διακρίσεως καὶ λύπης [καὶ] κοινωνοῦντα, ὅπερ ἐστὶν εὐεργεσία καθαρά. κρείττων δ᾿ ἐστὶ τούτου ὁ τοῦ κυρίου λελεγμένος ἐν ἄλλῳ χωρίῳ· »παντὶ τῷ αἰτοῦντί σε δίδου·« θεοῦ γὰρ ὄντως ἡ τοιαύτη φιλοδωρία.
thought_title: The reward of receiving Christ's little ones
orientation: Clement is quoting Jesus' sayings about receiving the poor and lowly as receiving Christ himself, and is now explaining that the reward for such reception is eternal.
pass_a_gloss: And elsewhere: "The one who receives you receives me, and the one who does not receive you rejects me." These he names both children and little ones and infants and friends and small ones here, in view of their future greatness above. "Do not despise," he says, "one of these small ones; for their angels always see the face of my Father in the heavens." And in another place: "Do not be afraid, little flock; for your Father was pleased to hand over to you the kingdom" of the heavens. In the same way he says that the least in the kingdom of the heavens, that is his own disciple, is greater than John, the greatest among those born of women. And again: "The one who receives a righteous person or a prophet in the name of a righteous person or a prophet will receive that one's reward. But the one who gives a disciple a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple will not lose the reward." Therefore this reward alone is not lost. And again: "Make for yourselves friends from the worldly wealth, so that when it fails, they may receive you into the eternal tents." He declares that by nature every possession, which a person himself possesses for himself as being his own and does not lay down for the common use of those in need, is unjust, but from this injustice it is possible to work both a just deed and a saving one, to give rest to one of those who have an eternal tent with the Father. See first that he has not commanded you to be asked, nor to wait to be troubled, but yourself to seek those who will be well treated and who are worthy to be disciples of the Savior. Beautiful then is also the saying of the apostle: "For God loves a cheerful giver," one who rejoices in giving and does not sow sparingly, so that he may not also reap in the same way. One who shares without grumbling and without doubting and without grief, which is pure beneficence. But better than this is the saying of the Lord spoken in another place: "Give to everyone who asks you." For such generosity is truly of God.

choices.why: The glossary requires this rendering for the term, preserving the sense of wealth that can be used to make friends for eternal dwellings.
Literal rendering of σκηνάς as 'tents' preserves the image of dwelling places, matching the following section's use of 'eternal tent'.
Standard rendering of the Pauline quotation, preserving the adjective's sense of gladness in giving.
The compound means love of giving; 'generosity' captures the disposition Clement attributes to God.

pass_b_english: And in another place he says, "Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever rejects you rejects me" (Matthew 10:40). These he calls children, little ones, infants, and friends, and small here in comparison with their future greatness above. "Do not despise one of these little ones," he says, "for their angels continually see the face of my Father in heaven" (Matthew 18:10). And elsewhere: "Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father was pleased to hand over to you the kingdom of heaven" (Luke 12:32). In the same way he says that the least in the kingdom of heaven—that is, his own disciple—is greater than John, the greatest among those born of women. And again: "Whoever receives a righteous person or a prophet in the name of a righteous person or a prophet will receive that person's reward. And whoever gives a disciple a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple will not lose his reward" (Matthew 10:41-42). This reward alone, then, is one that is not lost. And again: "Make friends for yourselves by means of worldly wealth, so that when it fails, they may receive you into the eternal tents" (Luke 16:9). By nature he declares that every possession which a person keeps for himself as his own and does not place in common for those in need is unrighteous; yet from this unrighteousness it is possible to produce a deed that is both righteous and saving—to give rest to one of those who have an eternal tent with the Father.

Observe first that he has not commanded you to wait to be asked or to be pestered, but to seek him himself, those who will fare well, being worthy disciples of the Savior. The apostle's word is good: "God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7)—one who rejoices in giving and does not sow sparingly, so that he may not reap in the same way; one who shares without grumbling, division, or grief, which is pure beneficence. But better than this is what the Lord said in another place: "Give to everyone who asks you" (Luke 6:30). For such generosity is truly God's own.

problems.ruling: διακρίσεως means division/discrimination; 'hesitation' misleads readers about the intended contrast with pure beneficence.

fixed: Changed 'hesitation' to 'division' for διακρίσεως, which means division or discrimination, not hesitation.

problems.why: Same Luke 16:9 phrase rendered three different ways; reader may miss the connection.
